title: Kinetic Studio
kind: Own lab · motion graphics in code
summary: My lab of motion-graphics trailers made in code: picture and sound are generated live in the browser, on an in-house engine with a single timeline that can be frozen at any second. This portfolio's trailer is built with its kit.

facts.v: My own project, built with a trailer agent
Hub · 31 trailers · engine, recipes and sound
Public lab: repo on GitHub, deploy to GitHub Pages

tldr.v: Product trailers with no video editor, no stock footage and no recorded audio. Every piece is code: it is edited as data and can be frozen at any frame.
One paused master timeline drives picture and sound. Scenes are recipes that return their duration, and the music is a list of notes.
31 trailers in the hub and this portfolio's 112 s trailer. It is a lab: it has no tests and the kit is copied into every folder.

p: Kinetic Studio is my motion-graphics lab. Each trailer is a web page drawn live: type, shapes, canvas particles, 3D scenes in WebGL and a soundtrack synthesised on the spot with WebAudio.

Each idea in the catalogue asks the engine for something different: variable type, 120,000 particles on the GPU, a story with public data and its source cited on screen, vertical formats, or an interactive trailer where scrolling is time.
list: A hub with the library: generative SVG posters with a fixed seed (identical on every load) and a live, silent preview on hover.
31 trailers in the hub (32 folders): 29 are made with the kit alone and 2 are commercials that animate real captures of a demo.
Adding up the catalogue: 1,430 seconds of film and 272 scenes.
I use it for pieces of my own products (four HandyX spots) and for this site's «Meet Ignacio» trailer.

p: A trailer is a configuration file. Each scene names a recipe, and the recipe returns how long it lasts: that way the engine knows the second each thing starts at and adds it to a single, paused GSAP timeline.

The music is data too: the score is a function that returns every note with its second and its voice, and that same list plays live, can be rendered offline and can move the picture on the beat. There are 23 synthesised voices and no audio files.

diagram.title: One timeline drives everything
diagram.caption: The Kinetic Studio engine (each trailer's js/engine.js). Picture and sound read the same timeline: when it moves, they move together. The warm-up pass was added by this portfolio's trailer.

recipes.label: Recipes
recipes.note: Each scene is a recipe: it gets the director, its start second and its options, and returns how long it lasts. A missing recipe or duration stops the engine with an error.

tl.label: Master timeline
tl.note: One, and paused. With ?⁠t=seconds in the URL any frame stays frozen: useful to review frame by frame and to export.

warm.label: Warm-up
warm.note: Before playing, it walks the film once behind a cover, a frame every 1.5 s: each scene's first frame is the expensive one.

image.label: Picture
image.note: Canvas layers are pure functions of the animated state: moving the timeline moves the canvas too, with no hidden state.

p: A trailer agent builds the trailers on top of the kit. The rest of the way is mechanical, with guards so a mistake doesn't get published.
pipeline.title: Eight steps, from a folder to a preview
pipeline.caption: Per the README and scripts/adopt-trailer.mjs. CI only builds and publishes from main: there are no checks on PRs.

steps.d: Creates trailers/<id>/ with its own copy of the kit: engine, sound and recipes.
Replaces the classic <script> tags with a main.ts that has one import per file, in order.
Scenes, palette, fonts and music: the only file you normally touch.
Calls each recipe with its start second and lets the music join at the end.
Poster and preview seconds, duration and number of scenes.
Strict tsc and Vite. A plugin stops the build if a local classic <script> is left.
Every push to main builds the hub and publishes it to GitHub Pages.
An iframe with ?⁠embed plays silently on hover.

p: The most demanding use of the kit is the «Meet Ignacio» trailer that opens this site. It uses the Kinetic engine with a single two-line change (inside the portfolio there are no single-letter shortcuts, per WCAG 2.1.4) and adds its own recipes, a mode to live inside the page and the warm-up pass.

In act 5, eleven views of real components from my projects are rebuilt in code (HTML, CSS and SVG animated with GSAP), with no screenshots. In act 6, each of the 17 technologies is an animation that shows what it does, with a fixed note on where I used it.
It is not all code: act 4 plays a recorded clip of the CompliA demo, and the HandyX views use four brand illustrations.

items.d: The same in Spanish and English

film.note: The portfolio's tests pin them: the e2e test expects a 112.00 s duration and the unit tests require 15 scenes, 11 views and 17 technologies with the same texts in both languages. I ran the unit tests on 10/28/2026: green.

host.h: How it plugs into the portfolio
p: The trailer is not bundled with the site: it is a static kit page inside a same-origin iframe, and the player is a chunk that only downloads on the click.
Browsers only let audio play and fullscreen start from a user gesture. So the audio context is created inside the click and the iframe borrows it.

seq.title: From the click to the end of the film
seq.caption: Messages travel with postMessage, only within the same origin: the trailer checks the origin, and the portfolio also checks that the message comes from its own iframe. Visitors who prefer reduced motion get a text version: no sound, no fullscreen.

items.why: If everything hangs off one timeline and each recipe returns its duration, the film is deterministic and you can jump to any second. That enables frame-by-frame review with ?⁠t=, the hub previews, frame-exact export and offline audio rendering.

items.t: Canvas as a function of state
items.why: Particles and the tunnel are drawn from animated parameters, with no hidden per-frame state: moving the timeline moves the canvas. When the playhead jumps, motion-blur streaks are switched off so no trails are left behind.

items.t: The music is a list of events
items.why: The same list plays live, renders offline with a fixed seed and can move the picture on the beat. In the offline render, voices are created just in time: creating them all up front made every audio block hundreds of times slower.

items.t: The expensive frame first, behind a cover
items.why: Each scene's first frame is the costly one (styles, split text, fonts, the first paint of a big view): that is where the cuts stuttered. The portfolio's trailer walks the film once before playing, so playback only repeats work already done.
items.alt: Canvas particles and animated chromatic shadows in that trailer: they went, and each act's background moves on the compositor.

items.why: Recipes are ES modules that talk through window, and Vite only bundles GSAP and Three.js from npm: trailers built by the agent work unchanged. Only a trailer that imports Three.js downloads it, and strict execution order keeps a shared chunk from running before the engine (it broke two pages).

items.t: Guards at build time and at run time
items.why: A Vite plugin stops the build if a page loads a local classic <script>. In the HandyX spots, ?⁠audit walks every tween and flags any property other than transform or opacity, and a scene that lasts differently from its storyboard stops the film from being built.

p: To keep the portfolio's trailer from stuttering: the warm-up pass, each act's background moved on the compositor, and no canvas particles or animated chromatic shadows. The engine's determinism was tested by reaching the same frame three ways.
The repo has no test suite: the build runs tsc in strict mode before Vite, and the JavaScript recipes are not type-checked.

items.d: Average frame of the portfolio's trailer (before: 29 ms)
Moments identical bit for bit, reached three ways
The largest difference in the other two, out of 2,073,600 and by one colour level

quality.note: Performance: lab measurement on 10/28/2026 in Chromium without a GPU, walking the whole film; not field data. Determinism: Kinetic's hash test (exports/hash.json) opens the same second from 0, from the end and from slightly before, and compares the captures by SHA-256 and pixel by pixel.

kinetic.alt: A frame of the KINETIC trailer: the word KINETIC, huge and white, on a dark violet background, crossed by a thin circle, with the line «A motion study in form, color & time», three coloured shapes and HUD marks in the corners.
kinetic.caption: A frame of the KINETIC trailer, taken from its MP4 export. Everything you see is drawn with code.

list: The kit is copied into every folder and has drifted: 30 copies of engine.js in 10 different versions and 30 of audio.js in 9 (counted by hash). Unifying it is next.
The MP4 export cannot be reproduced from the repo alone: the exporter lives outside it, in the kit's local tools.
There are no tests, and CI only builds and publishes from main.

The engine's embed mode accepts messages from any origin and answers anyone. The impact is low (it only moves a preview, no data), but it does not check the origin. The portfolio's trailer does not use that mode.
The film grain uses fresh randomness on every load: frames are identical within a load, not necessarily across loads.
The exported renders (MP4, GIF and WAV) are committed to git even though they are not published.

status.h: Status and what I don't claim
list: Public lab: 31 trailers in the hub, one more unlisted folder and the first version of KINETIC as a legacy page.
I don't claim it is all code: two commercials animate real captures of a demo, and the portfolio's trailer has a video clip and four illustrations.
I don't claim bit-exact deterministic export: the test gave 2 of 4 moments identical and 2 differing by one colour level.
The exporter is not in the repo, and the repo has no licence: it is not open source.
The performance figures are lab numbers, in Chromium without a GPU.
